content: The diagnosis and treatment of tuberculosis (TB) have led to an increase in TB-related deaths, with 2 million deaths reported in 2019. Additionally, there were 214,000 deaths among HIV-positive individuals in 2020, up from 209,000 in 2019. This combined total has returned to levels observed in 2017. Between 2019 and 2020, there was a 15% reduction in the number of people receiving treatment for drug-resistant TB, decreasing from 177,100 to 150,359, which represents only about one-third of those in need. In 2018, 132,222 cases of multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) and 25,681 cases of pre-extensively drug-resistant TB (pre-XDR-TB) or extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) were detected, totaling 157,903 cases. This marked a significant 22% decline from the 201,997 cases detected in 2019. This reduction aligns with an 18% decrease in the total number of newly diagnosed TB cases and a 17% decrease in bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB cases between 2019 and 2020. Globally, 150,359 individuals with MDR/RR-TB were enrolled in treatment in 2020, a 15% decrease from 177,100 in 2019. This level of enrollment corresponds to approximately one in three people who develop MDR/RR-TB annually. On a more positive note, treatment success rates have improved. In 2018, the global treatment success rate for MDR/RR-TB was 59%, reflecting steady progress from 50% in 2012. Drug-resistant TB remains a global challenge, with access to treatment often hindered by the long, toxic, and expensive nature of current regimens. There is a pressing need for more effective and shorter treatment regimens to optimize outcomes, minimize adverse events, and prevent the development of additional drug resistance. The World Health Organization (WHO) has updated its consolidated guidelines on TB treatment, particularly for drug-resistant TB, in 2022. The BPaL regimen (bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid) was evaluated in the TB-PRACTECAL trial, which included patients with MDR/RR-TB, with or without fluoroquinolone resistance (pre-XDR-TB). This regimen was compared to various local standard-of-care (SoC) regimens, including injectable-containing regimens lasting 9–12 months, older WHO regimens lasting 18–24 months, and all-oral regimens lasting 9–20 months. The BPaL regimen demonstrated potential improvements in treatment success, reduced failure and recurrence rates, and lower mortality and loss to follow-up. However, it may lead to increased amplification of drug resistance, and the evidence remains highly uncertain. The BPaL regimen offers a shorter treatment duration (approximately 6 months) compared to control regimens, which range from 9 to 24 months. The pill burden is also lower with BPaL, though the exact reduction depends on the comparator regimen. The WHO Guideline Development Group (GDG) judged that BPaL may have substantial desirable effects, with trivial undesirable effects, despite the very low certainty of evidence. The trial faced several limitations, including imbalances in measured covariates (e.g., prior TB or drug-resistant TB), small sample sizes, lack of blinding, and early termination for benefit, all of which may introduce bias. Additionally, the use of multiple comparator regimens across sites contributed to inconsistencies in treatment outcomes between countries (e.g., Belarus, South Africa, and Uzbekistan). These factors led to downgrading the certainty of evidence for some outcomes. Pretomanid, a key component of the BPaL regimen, has been evaluated for safety. Rodent studies indicated direct testicular toxicity, while monkey studies showed no direct testicular toxicity, with abnormal sperm findings attributed to declining physical condition. Clinical studies revealed no changes in hormone levels (FSH, LH, Inhibin B) consistent with testicular toxicity. A paternity survey involving 38 men who underwent pretomanid treatment for 4–6 months reported 44 children fathered, suggesting no significant reproductive toxicity. An ongoing semen study is further investigating this aspect. The WHO GDG determined that the balance of health effects likely favors the BPaL regimen due to its shorter duration, lower pill burden, and reduced complexity. The regimen is also cost-saving in most settings, primarily due to reduced time in care, fewer outpatient visits, inpatient bed-days, and laboratory tests. The GDG judged the reduction in costs to range from moderate to large. However, the certainty of evidence remains very low, and further research is needed to confirm these findings.
